Lakshmi has also sought the court’s intervention to obtain documents and information that she alleges have been withheld despite repeated requests.Lakshmi compelled to approach court: MallikaThe suit concerns the ownership and division of joint family assets and does not seek to interfere with the operations of any company, the statement said. Lakshmi has an interest in the continued strength of the businesses and believes any division of assets can be implemented in an orderly manner in accordance with the law.Supporting her claim, her mother, Mallika Srinivasan, said Lakshmi had been compelled to approach the court after the response to her notice failed to recognise her rights and no progress has been made towards amicable resolution. “As a mother, to me, a son and daughter are equal in every respect,” she said.Lakshmi Venu’s claim is based on her interpretation of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as amended in 2005, which recognises daughters’ rights in coparcenary property. The assets she seeks to partition include interests held through the VS Trust and other holding entities in businesses such as TVS Holdings, TVS Motor Company, TVS Credit Services and Sundaram-Clayton, allocated to the Venu Srinivasan branch under the 2020 TVS Group family arrangement.She contends the arrangement did not constitute a partition within her immediate family and that no division or settlement of its assets has been initiated or concluded.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: 85-year-old man sought to evict his son and daughter-in-law from self-acquired Delhi home, but authorities rejected plea over lack of proof of harassment; Delhi High Court overturns their orders and gives couple four weeks to vacate
articles.summary: Can children forcefully continue to live in their parents’ self-acquired property if the latter ask them to vacate?
articles.body: Can children forcefully continue to live in their parents’ self-acquired property if the latter ask them to vacate? An 85-year-old man has secured relief with the Delhi High Court asking his son and daughter-in-law to vacate the property.The court held that a senior citizen seeking eviction under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, does not necessarily have to prove that his children have ill-treated him.What the case is aboutAn elderly man owns a flat which he acquired from the Delhi Development Authority in 1980 and converted it into freehold in 2000. His eldest son and daughter-in-law had been living there since their marriage in 2003.The man claimed that he had asked the couple to arrange alternative accommodation after his second son married in 2005 and his youngest son married in 2008. He alleged that the couple refused to leave, that their behaviour towards him deteriorated over the years and that they stopped supporting him financially. He further claimed that their harassment intensified after his wife died in November 2020.The father alleged that in 2022, the couple threatened him and assaulted his youngest son. He said he filed a police complaint and subsequently approached the authorities under the 2007 Act, seeking eviction and maintenance.The District Magistrate rejected his application in 2023, observing that the allegations had not been proved and that the Act was being used to resolve a business dispute between the sons.The father appealed and in June 2025, the Divisional Commissioner set aside the original order and sent the matter back for reconsideration because the first inquiry had not determined whether the complaint was genuine.A fresh enquiry report again concluded that harassment had not been established. The District Magistrate rejected the application and the Divisional Commissioner upheld that decision in April 2026.The father then approached the Delhi High Court. His counsel argued that, as the property's absolute owner, he was entitled to live there peacefully and that proof of ill-treatment was not a prerequisite for eviction.The respondents disputed his account. Their counsel argued that the complaint had been made at the instance of the father's younger son amid a business dispute between the brothers. They also maintained that they had been looking after the father and had offered to pay him Rs 15,000 a month as maintenance.Why Delhi High Court asked son & daughter to vacateThe Delhi High Court noted that the father's ownership was undisputed. The son and daughter-in-law had not claimed ownership rights over the property and were living there because of their relationship with him. The father had also made it clear that he no longer wished to share his home with them.The court relied on the Supreme Court's August 4, 2026, decision in Ravi Kant Gupta v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors., which recognised that tribunals under the Senior Citizens Act could order eviction where necessary to protect a senior citizen.It also referred to the Delhi High Court's earlier ruling in Pritam Singh v. Government of NCT of Delhi & Ors., which recognised that proof of ill-treatment was not invariably necessary if the property needed protection so the senior citizen could live peacefully.The court found that the authorities had made proof of harassment an essential condition without considering whether the property needed protection.It criticised the first enquiry report for being inconclusive, observing: “A report which is, on its own showing, inconclusive could not have formed the basis of a finding that the allegations of harassment stood disproved.”The authorities had also failed to adequately consider the father's repeated police complaints and an earlier High Court direction requiring the police to assist him against any threat from the respondents.The existence of a business dispute between the brothers, the court said, could not by itself justify rejecting the father's grievance.As the judgment put it: “Merely because there may also exist a business dispute between the sons of the petitioner, the same, by itself, cannot be a ground to hold that the grievance of the petitioner is not genuine, or to deny him the protection afforded under the Act.”Ultimately, the High Court held that an elderly parent should not be compelled to share his home against his wishes when the relationship has deteriorated to the point of prolonged litigation.The Delhi High Court observed: “At the age of 85 years, the petitioner is entitled to live in his own house peacefully and with dignity.”The court set aside the Divisional Commissioner's order and the District Magistrate's order. It directed the son and daughter-in-law to vacate the property within four weeks and instructed the concerned Station House Officer to provide the necessary assistance if required.Adnan Siddiqui, Partner at King Stubb & Kasiva, told ET that father prevailed before the Delhi High Court because he is the absolute owner of the DDA flat.Neither his son nor his daughter-in-law has any independent interest in the property, as they were permitted to live there only with his consent. After the father decided that they could no longer stay in the flat because of the harassment he had faced, the Delhi High Court upheld his decision.Siddiqui says: "This case is significant as it highlights that, in addition to aspects relating to property, the entitlement of older people to live in their own home is also associated with their safety, and both mental and physical wellbeing."Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Judge blocks Trump’s FCC from targeting ABC stations: ‘This is not a close case’
articles.summary: Siding with Disney in a dramatic First Amendment case, a federal judge has barred the Trump administration from taking further action against ABC’s local TV stations.
articles.body: Siding with Disney in a dramatic First Amendment case, a federal judge has barred the Trump administration from taking further action against ABC’s local TV stations. On Wednesday, US District Judge Loren AliKhan issued the preliminary injunction that Disney has been seeking against the Federal Communications Commission, chaired by Brendan Carr, a close ally of President Donald Trump. “This is not a close case,” AliKhan wrote in her decision, which also denied the FCC’s motion to dismiss Disney’s lawsuit. The injunction means that the FCC can’t continue its early review of ABC’s station licenses while the legal process plays out. After weighing the evidence, the judge concluded that Disney’s lawyers “sufficiently cast the early license renewal proceedings as a retaliatory act.” The ruling is a clear victory for Disney, which went to court in August to defend its ABC stations from the FCC’s pressure campaign. The stations fall under the FCC’s purview because they broadcast over the public airwaves. Disney’s lawsuit documented the FCC’s unusual steps to investigate and challenge ABC’s stations. “The administration has steadily increased the pressure” on ABC, the suit stated, “culminating in the present threat to the broadcasting licenses of the eight ABC owned stations.” ABC’s licenses weren’t due for renewal for several years, but in April, Carr ordered the company to file early-renewal paperwork, something that the FCC virtually never does. At the same time, Trump publicly pressured ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel, and the network ignored his demands. Carr claimed that the license review was related to an ongoing FCC probe of Disney’s diversity, equity, and inclusion efforts. But former FCC officials said that explanation didn’t make sense, and Disney argued that it was just a pretext. Disney said the court’s intervention was necessary to stop an “extraordinary assault on free speech.” AliKhan heard arguments from both sides in October. FCC lawyers argued that the District Court lacked jurisdiction, but on Wednesday she wrote that Disney had established jurisdiction. “No one doubts that the commission may enforce the law in the manner it sees fit,” the judge wrote. “But in doing so, defendants may not retaliate against or punish plaintiffs and other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech.” AliKhan wrote that Carr “has taken President Trump’s rhetoric as his marching orders,” and “it is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel’s skit on social media and the very next day defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings.” An ABC spokesperson said: “Today’s decision is an important victory for the First Amendment. We thank the court for its careful consideration.” In a statement, an FCC spokesperson said the “decision granting Disney’s motion is wrong on the facts and wrong on the law,” and said the commission “looks forward to prevailing in full on this matter. We will continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations.” But the FCC’s lone Democratic commissioner, Anna Gomez, cheered the judge’s decision, saying it showed that “this FCC is a paper tiger whose threats crumble when challenged by those willing to defend their rights.” Gomez, who publicly supported Disney’s lawsuit, said, “For nearly two years, the agency has weaponized its licensing authority to retaliate against broadcasters for exercising their right to free expression, and now a federal court has stepped in to put a check on that conduct.” Gomez urged other broadcasters to “take note” and follow Disney’s lead.

articles.title: Abrupt end to Kalyan-raj at Flipkart
articles.summary: BENGALURU: Flipkart group CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy, who helped turn around the homegrown e-commerce major when it was losing ground to Amazon, is leaving
articles.body: BENGALURU: Flipkart group CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy, who helped turn around the homegrown e-commerce major when it was losing ground to Amazon, is leaving after nearly a decade at the helm, amid differences with parent Walmart over listing plans and financial priorities.Krishnamurthy’s last working day will be Dec 4, just nine days after the announcement, according to an internal communication from Walmart International president and CEO Chris Nicholas to employees, reviewed by TOI. An emergency town hall was called on Wednesday, with the news of an abrupt leadership transition at one of India’s most valuable internet companies catching even senior leadership off guard.“Most of us were clueless. It’s so sudden since tension, if any, was not apparent,” a senior Flipkart executive told TOI.Sources in the know claimed Krishnamurthy and Walmart’s leadership differed over the timing of Flipkart’s public listing and providing liquidity to employees holding stock options. While an initial public offering (IPO) had been in the works for some time, Walmart has been pushing the company to improve its financial performance before going public.Chief product and technology officer Balaji Thiagarajan and the Flipkart board will lead the company in the interim. A successor will be announced in the coming weeks.Krishnamurthy’s association with Flipkart goes back nearly 15 years, when he left eBay to join Tiger Global, a key investor in the company. He served as Flipkart’s interim CFO in 2013-14 before returning to Tiger.His return in mid-2016 came during the most difficult period in Flipkart’s history. Sales growth had stagnated, repeated valuation markdowns hurt investor sentiment, senior executives were leaving and Amazon had committed $5 billion to India.Focusing on smartphones, large appliances and branded fashion, Krishnamurthy helped Flipkart regain market share, demonstrating an Indian startup could hold its own against a global giant. Co-founder Binny Bansal had replaced Sachin Bansal as CEO in 2016.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? Join the TOI Money Masterclass.

Electricity demand, diesel consumption, toll collections and digital payment value rose 21.9 per cent, 12 per cent, 12.3 per cent and 22.9 per cent, respectively. articles.title: US approves Musk's SpaceX plan to deploy 1 million satellites for AI data centres in space
articles.summary: The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has authorised Elon Musk's SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million satellites that will function as data centres
articles.body: The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has authorised Elon Musk's SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million satellites that will function as data centres in space, as the company seeks to meet rapidly growing demand for artificial intelligence computing.The FCC said on Wednesday it had approved SpaceX's proposed "Starmind" constellation of orbital computing modules which would process massive amounts of data and transmit it back to Earth.SpaceX had earlier sought permission to deploy up to 1 million satellites to support AI computing infrastructure in space.The FCC said the approval would allow SpaceX "to pioneer emergent technology that advances American leadership in space and artificial intelligence".Data centres are the physical backbone of artificial intelligence, requiring enormous amounts of electricity to run and cool computing systems.SpaceX has proposed powering its orbital data centres using solar energy, arguing that the technology could significantly reduce energy costs and the environmental impact associated with conventional data centres on Earth."By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centers," SpaceX told the FCC.The company plans to use its next-generation Starship rocket which is currently under development to deploy the constellation.The ambitious proposal depends heavily on Starship's ability to lower launch costs and carry large numbers of satellites into orbit.FCC chairman Brendan Carr said the approval would help the US strengthen its position in artificial intelligence and expand computing infrastructure."America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence. Under President Trump's leadership, the United States is moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers lasting benefits for the American people. The FCC supercharges that effort today by granting, for the first time ever, authorization to deploy 1 million orbital compute modules for data centers in space. This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth," Carr said."Compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership in SI. By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment. This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," he added.The FCC has also approved SpaceX's request to establish backup communications for its optical network. The system will use radiofrequency links for emergency telemetry, tracking and command operations, as well as backup connectivity across the satellite network.The approval allows communications in the 18.8–19.3 GHz bands for downlinks and 28.6–29.1 GHz bands for uplinks.It remains unclear whether SpaceX will eventually deploy the entire constellation. There are currently around 17,000 satellites in orbit, and deploying 1 million would represent an unprecedented expansion of satellite infrastructure, Reuters reported.Satellite operators often seek approval for larger constellations than they ultimately intend to deploy, allowing flexibility as their technology and business plans evolve.SpaceX had previously sought approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites. The network currently has more than 11,000 satellites in orbit.Amazon's satellite unit Leo and other competitors have questioned SpaceX's proposed constellation arguing that deploying the entire network could take centuries and that the company may not launch all the satellites it has sought approval for.Carr dismissed the criticism in March, saying, "Amazon should focus on getting Amazon's house in order with their own launches and their own satellite constellation, rather than worrying about other people that are actually out there ​launching satellites at the pace and cadence that SpaceX is."Under the approval, SpaceX must begin deployment by November 2033 and launch at least 10% of the approved constellation, or 100,000 satellites by November 2035 and deploy 50% by November 2038.Money habits form by age 7. articles.body: US president Donald Trump’s investment portfolios traded shares of chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times between January and September, with the value of his holdings potentially rising by as much as $15 million after the company’s stock surged following the return of chief executive Jensen Huang.A review of Trump’s financial disclosures by BBC Verify found that his portfolios bought between $5.2 million and $17 million worth of Nvidia shares during the first nine months of the year, while selling between $4.4 million and $12 million worth.The filings, submitted to the US Office of Government Ethics, report transactions in broad value ranges rather than exact amounts, making it impossible to establish precisely how much Nvidia stock Trump traded or how many shares he held.Trump’s latest disclosure, submitted on November 5, indicated that he could have held as many as 370,000 Nvidia shares as of September 30.Nvidia shares surged more than 30% on Monday after the company’s board reinstated Huang as CEO, potentially increasing the value of Trump’s investment by $15 million.The rally followed Trump’s public involvement in Huang’s reinstatement. The president told CNBC he had spoken to Nvidia’s board and “made the deal” to bring the executive back. Nvidia said it had received input from senior US government officials before deciding Huang’s return posed no national security risk.Trump’s portfolios also held between $12.5 million and $58 million worth of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025, according to the disclosures.The White House has said Trump’s stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties, and that neither the president nor his family can direct or influence investment decisions.The frequent trading of Nvidia shares has nevertheless raised questions about potential conflicts of interest, particularly given Trump’s role in the company’s leadership decision and the administration’s oversight of advanced chip exports to China.Nvidia has become one of the world’s most valuable companies amid the boom in artificial intelligence. Its shares account for more than 6% of the S&P 500, making it one of the most influential stocks in the index.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? articles.title: Anthropic CEO Amodei denies wanting humanity to ‘surrender’ free will to AI
articles.summary: Dario Amodei’s remarks come amid predictions that AI may soon match or surpass human intelligence.
articles.body:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has denied believing that humanity should “surrender” control to artificial intelligence amid predictions that models potentially far exceeding human intelligence are imminent.

In a lengthy post on X on Wednesday, Amodei said he does not support surrendering “human free will” to AI and has long argued that the frontier technology should be subject to “legitimate democratic processes”.

“If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years,” Amodei said, responding to an Axios report about a purported “consensus” inside Anthropic that some decision-making authority should be passed to the technology.

“But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.”

Amodei’s remarks come amid a flurry of commentary by top industry executives suggesting that AI will soon match or surpass human intelligence.

The prospect of AI that equals or outperforms the best human minds – referred to as artificial general intelligence (AGI) and artificial super-intelligence (ASI), respectively – has fuelled intense debate in Silicon Valley and beyond about whether such technology can be harnessed for good without exposing humanity to catastrophic harm.

AI safety advocates have raised fears that models being developed by firms such as Anthropic, which made history last week in the biggest initial public offering of all time, could slip out of human control, particularly once systems start improving without human input, a process known as recursive self-improvement.

In his X post, Amodei criticised commentary he said conflated the idea of AI taking over specific tasks with surrendering control in a “grand sense of global governance”.

“This is not AI ‘running the world’, but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end,” Amodei said.

“Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc.”

“It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives,” he added. “But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.”

Citing unnamed sources, Axios reported on Wednesday that Amodei and other Anthropic executives believe it would be irrational “or even unethical” not to hand over authority to AI for tasks it can do better than humans, such as curing diseases.

David Krueger, the founder of Evitable, a nonprofit that campaigns against the development of ASI, said Anthropic should pause its work if Amodei is genuinely concerned about humanity losing control of frontier models.

“We don’t have to consciously surrender control to AI to lose it. As AI becomes increasingly capable, there will be mounting pressure to push humans out of decision-making roles across society,” Krueger told Al Jazeera.

“Meanwhile, researchers at Dario’s own company are warning that AI capabilities are advancing faster than our ability to control them. We need an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development.”

While there is no universally agreed-upon definition of AGI or ASI, key tech industry figures have over the past week suggested that the milestones are near.

Google DeepMind’s chief AGI scientist and cofounder, Shane Legg, said on Wednesday he believes there is a more than 50 percent chance that “minimal” AGI arrives before 2028.

“We’re getting close now,” Legg said on X.

On Sunday, Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, said ASI is “arriving” , pointing to the announcement that an Anthropic employee had used Claude to solve the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most difficult problems in mathematics.

“How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in,” Wang said on X.

articles.body: Stock Market Today: Indian shares set to extend gains Indian benchmark indices are likely to open higher, extending their recent rally as record foreign fund inflows push markets closer to erasing year-to-date losses. GIFT Nifty futures were trading at 26,061.5 at 8:01am, signalling a positive opening for the Nifty 50, which closed at 25,819.25 on Wednesday. US tariffs will remain in focus after the Trump administration proposed levies on imports from 14 trading partners, including India, to address what it calls structural excess industrial capacity. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Washington would cap tariffs on Indian imports at 17% if a trade deal is reached with New Delhi. In the absence of an agreement, the tariff rate would rise to 25%, adding to uncertainty over India's trade outlook..Stock Market Today: Oil rises on supply concerns Crude oil prices rose in early Asian trade on Thursday, extending gains from the previous session amid supply concerns after Yemen's Houthis claimed an attack on Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery and at least two ships reportedly struck Iranian mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude futures rose 10 cents, or 0.1%, to $94.71 a barrel by 0137 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude gained 35 cents, or 0.4%, to $84.03 a barrel. WTI will not have a settlement on Thursday due to the US Thanksgiving holiday. On Wednesday, Brent crude surged 3.5%, while WTI climbed 2% after Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis claimed attacks on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery and Riyadh's financial district..Asian markets rally as US tariff concerns ease Asian markets rallied on Thursday as investors found the latest US tariff proposals less alarming than expected, while the Thanksgiving holiday offered some respite from the recent AI-driven selloff. Japan's Nikkei rose 1.6%, South Korea's benchmark gained 1.9% and Taiwan advanced 1.4%. Asian markets outside Japan climbed 1.5%, while Chinese blue-chip stocks added 0.6%. The rebound came after steep monthly losses, with Japan down 8%, South Korea 16% and Taiwan 15%. The White House's proposed tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union, are unlikely to be imposed before February or March and will not be added to tariffs introduced in July, easing immediate concerns..Wall Street recovers most early losses as pullback in AI stocks eases Stocks on Wall Street closed moderately lower Wednesday after another punishing pullback in AI stocks lost momentum as the day went on, reversing much of the market’s losses. The S&P 500 index fell 0.3% after having been down as much as 3.2% earlier in the day. The Nasdaq composite finished 0.6% lower. At one point, it had been down as much as 4.6%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.3%. The market pared its losses even as a report raised more worries about high inflation and as President Donald Trump plans to escalate the U.S. trade war with major trading partners. AI stocks lost ground for a second day following Monday’s relief rally over the surprise reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. Stocks have been generally falling since setting an all-time high last month as worries grow that AI stock prices have grown unjustifiably high. The market turnaround came as some of the biggest tech companies bounced back from steep drops. Nvidia, which was down more than 9% at one point, closed with a 3.9% loss. Broadcom, which had dropped more than 6%, ended just 0.1% lower, while Microsoft came back from a more than 3% slide to finish down 1.2%. Anthropic bounced back from an early drop to close with a 1.1% gain. Still, since soaring to $115 per share on the day it became the first major frontier lab to go public, Anthropic shares have tumbled by about 28%. Roughly three quarters of the stocks in the S&P 500 rose, although the pullback in technology stocks kept the index in the red..Stock market today: Sensex ends over 1,500 point after 2,000 point surge, Nifty50 crosses 25,800 Indian benchmark indices staged a sharp rebound on Wednesday, recovering from Monday's selloff as foreign fund inflows, easing crude oil prices and buying in heavyweight banking stocks lifted sentiment, despite weak global cues and concerns over AI-linked stocks. The gains followed Monday's sharp decline, when the Sensex plunged 1,483.72 points, or 1.77%, to 82,435.99, while the Nifty fell 450.95 points, or 1.75%, to 25,349.65. articles.title: RBI continues to bring back gold to India as it repatriates 60 tonnes more of yellow metal, India now houses 84% of its 880.52 metric tonnes gold reserves while remaining are with Bank of England and Bank for International Settlements
articles.summary: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has been bringing back India’s gold stored abroad for some time now and it continued to shift the yellow metal reserves
articles.body: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has been bringing back India’s gold stored abroad for some time now and it continued to shift the yellow metal reserves back even in this year.However, what is interesting to note is that gold accounted for a smaller proportion of the country's overall foreign exchange reserves at the end of September, data released on Wednesday showed.Despite the increase in gold held within India, its share in total foreign exchange reserves fell to 14.38% at the end of September, compared with 16.7% six months earlier.RBI moves back most of India’s gold reservesAccording to the RBI's latest half-yearly report, India's gold reserves stood at 880.52 metric tonnes at the end of September. Of this, 740.13 metric tonnes, equivalent to 84% of the total, were held within the country.The remaining 140.39 metric tonnes were kept with the Bank of England and the Bank for International Settlements.RBI repatriated around 60 tonnes of gold during April-September 2026. India has been progressively repatriating its gold holdings over the past two years amid rising geopolitical risks. In March, 77% of the country's gold reserves were held domestically.India’s forex reservesIndia's foreign exchange reserves totalled $705.3 billion, according to the latest data released by the central bank on Friday.When reserves stood at $668.6 billion at the end of June, they were sufficient to cover 9.8 months of imports, the RBI said.The ratio of short-term debt to foreign exchange reserves climbed to 23% at the end of June 2026, up from 21.6% at the end of March. The ratio of volatile capital flows, including portfolio investments, to reserves also increased, reaching 68% at the end of June against 66.6% three months earlier.Most of India's foreign exchange reserves continue to be invested in securities issued by overseas governments. In addition, $35.95 billion was held as deposits with other central banks and the Bank for International Settlements, while $42.75 billion was deposited with commercial banks abroad."With the objective of exploring new strategies and products in reserve management while diversifying the portfolio, a small portion of the reserves is being managed by external asset managers," the RBI said.The period was marked by heightened geopolitical uncertainty, driven by the conflict in West Asia, interruptions to energy supplies and tighter monetary policies adopted by several major central banks.Global gold prices fell by around 9%, with the average price dropping from $4,721 per troy ounce in April 2026 to $4,319 in September."Prices responded to rising US Treasury yields, a stronger US dollar and expectations of tighter monetary policy. The decline occurred despite continued investor demand for gold as a safe-haven and for portfolio diversification," the report noted.India's overall foreign exchange reserves, meanwhile, grew by $46.67 billion during April-September 2026. They increased from $691.11 billion at the end of March to $737.78 billion at the end of September.Of the $608.26 billion in foreign currency assets held at the end of September, $529.57 billion was invested in securities. A further $35.95 billion was placed with other central banks and the BIS, while $42.75 billion was maintained as deposits with commercial banks overseas.The report also pointed to shifts in the composition of global foreign exchange reserves. The US dollar's share fell from 57.18% in the first quarter of 2026 to 56.70% in the second quarter. Over the same period, the euro's share rose from 20.04% to 20.60%.The RBI reiterated that protecting the safety of India's foreign exchange reserves and ensuring their liquidity remain the central priorities in managing the portfolio, with returns optimised within these parameters.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: South Korea’s central bank hikes interest rates amid AI chip boom
articles.summary: Bank of Korea raises key rate by 0.25 percent amid booming exports of semiconductors.
articles.body:
South Korea’s central bank has hiked interest rates as red-hot chip demand drives one of the Asian economy’s fastest expansions in more than a decade.

The Bank of Korea (BOK) on Thursday raised its key rate by 0.25 percent to 3.25 percent, citing strong domestic growth and above-target inflation.

Despite tensions in the Middle East, the global economy is expected to maintain a favourable growth trend due to “robust AI investment”, the BOK said in a statement.

Meanwhile, inflation is projected to “stay elevated for some time” amid the fallout of higher energy prices, the BOK said.

“Looking ahead, the global economy and financial markets will be affected by the AI investment outlook, by changes in monetary and fiscal policies in major economies, and by developments in the Middle East,” the central bank said.

South Korea’s inflation rate stood at 2.8 percent in October, above the BOK’s 2 percent target.

Citing expectations of sustained growth in exports and investment, the BOK raised its gross domestic product (GDP) growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 to 3.9 percent and 4.1 percent, respectively.

The BOK in August forecast that growth would reach 3.3 percent this year and 2.9 percent in 2027.

South Korea, which is home to top memory chip makers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, has been a major beneficiary of the multi-trillion-dollar AI investment boom.

South Korea’s exports rose 94 percent year-on-year in October to reach $115.3bn, following an all-time monthly record of $120.9bn in September.

Semiconductors accounted for nearly half of total exports, led by SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, which together control about 80 percent of the global market for high-bandwidth memory and 60 percent of the market for dynamic random-access memory, according to Counterpoint Research.

GDP increased 3.4 percent year-on-year in the July-September quarter, far outpacing forecasts.

Excluding the outlier years of the COVID-19 pandemic, Asia’s fourth-largest economy is on track for its strongest performance since 2010, when GDP expanded 6.2 percent.

After a tech-led sell-off the previous day, South Korea’s stock market rose on Thursday alongside a rebound in equities across the region.

Seoul’s Kospi closed up 0.3 percent, while the Nikkei 225 in Tokyo and the Taiex in Taipei finished 0.9 percent and 2.5 percent higher, respectively.

articles.title: Major discount chain collapses in insolvency, more than 11,000 jobs at risk
articles.summary: The chain Poundland was founded in 1990 and currently has more than 600 stores.
articles.body:
The British High Street, which is the local term for a city's main commercial thoroughfare and more metaphorically the nationwide brands that typically appear in central shopping areas, have faced a tough few years.

Fashion brands such as Claire's, River Island, and Russell and Bromley are all among the chains that collectively closed hundreds of stores across the United Kingdom in 2026 amid a sharp dropoff in sales.

Squeezed consumer budgets and a retail environment that moved increasingly online have both contributed to this period of sustained decline even in discount brands that had formerly been more resilient than the rest of the industry.

British discount variety chain Poundland collapses into administration

This week, value variety chain and fashion retailer Poundland made headlines after entering administration. The British term for the insolvency process that is the closest equivalent to a Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. requires a company unable to meet its financial obligations to hand over control to a court-appointed administrator who will typically explore restructuring options to avoid liquidation.

Founded by Dave Dodd and Steven Smith out of the West Midlands city of Walsall in 1990, Poundland expanded quickly to a national chain with more than 600 stores across the United Kingdom.

As an early player in stores selling low-cost versions of various popular grocery, toiletries, home, and household cleaning products, Poundland reached a mass audience quickly and went through different periods of loss and profit over the years.

But while Poundland went from reporting a loss of £68 million to profit of £18.1 million between 2025 and 2026 as a more value-driven consumer increasingly looked for affordable options of popular brands, a central sticking point for the brand's inability to find a new buyer is a £22.5 million shareholder loan that current owner Gordon Brothers inherited when it purchased Poundland from Pepco for a symbolic £1 in June 2025.

Poundland Managing Director Barry Williams sent staff a note saying that the company had "no alternative but to take this decision" to enter administration after talks with several potential bidders around a discount deal ultimately fell through at the eleventh hour and Gordon Brothers took away "all borrowing facilities and access to our bank accounts" at the end of October.

An increasingly uncertain future for the Poundland chain

"Under these circumstances, it is impossible for the board of directors to see how Poundland can continue to operate as a going concern," Williams' note reads further.

articles.title: Oil rises on supply concerns as Iran claims mine strikes on ships
articles.summary: SINGAPORE, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Crude oil prices rose on Thursday, extending gains from the previous session on supply concerns after Yemen's Houthis said they...
articles.body:
SINGAPORE, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Crude oil prices rose on Thursday, extending gains from the previous session on supply concerns after Yemen's Houthis said they had hit Saudi Arabia's largest ‌oil refinery and at least two ships hit Iranian mines in the Strait of ‌Hormuz.

Brent crude futures ( BZ=F ) were 10 cents, or 0.1%, higher at $94.71 a barrel by 0640 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures ​rose 31 cents, or 0.4%, to $83.99 a barrel. There will be no settlement for WTI on Thursday due to the US Thanksgiving holiday.

Prices rose for the third straight session on Thursday and are up about 5% this week, after plunging by around a quarter in the three weeks since the beginning of November. ‌Middle East exports have been increasing despite ⁠continued attacks on shipping, which triggered expectations of a global oil surplus this year.

Brent finished 3.5% higher in the previous session, while WTI climbed 2% after Yemen's ⁠Iran-aligned Houthis said they had attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery and Riyadh's financial district.

The refinery, Saudi Arabia's largest, is part of a complex that also serves as a major export terminal for Saudi crude, ​and analysts ​expect the latest Houthi attacks to increase the geopolitical ​risk premium.

At the same time, shipping has ‌been disrupted through the Strait of Hormuz, where oil supply had been recovering to near pre-war levels.

An oil tanker hit a naval mine and caught fire in a "restricted zone" in the strait on Wednesday, the semi-official Fars news agency cited an Iranian Army statement as saying. That report came after state media said two oil tankers struck mines and exploded in the strait on Wednesday.

"The broadening of the ‌Middle East conflict threatens to halt the recovery in oil ​flows in recent weeks. Persian Gulf crude exports rose last ​week but remain on a declining trend," ​said ANZ analyst Daniel Hynes.

OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on ‌November 29 to decide on their 2027 output ​policy, facing the challenge ​of balancing output with the United Arab Emirates no longer in the group, and with Iraq and Kazakhstan pressing OPEC+ to raise its estimate of their oil production capacity.

In the US, ​crude stocks rose by 1.1 million ‌barrels to 418.9 million barrels in the week ended November 20, the Energy Information ​Administration said, also supporting prices as analysts had expected a 1.5 million-barrel rise.

(Reporting by ​Sudarshan Varadhan; Editing by Sonali Paul and Lincoln Feast.)

articles.title: Artists are quitting Instagram and Facebook over fears AI will steal their work
articles.summary: A wave of AI-generated artwork is taking business away from creators and is especially prevalent on Meta-owned Instagram and Facebook.
articles.body: Matty Burnham, a watercolor artist in the United Kingdom, said he discovered a Pinterest account impersonating his illustration in 2024. The account created AI versions of his watercolors and listed them on fake profiles via Shopify, Facebook and Instagram, he told CNN. Although Burnham tracked the Pinterest account to Ho Chi Min City, Vietnam, he does not know who was behind it. It’s part of a wave of AI-generated artwork that’s taking business away from the creators themselves, and is especially prevalent on Meta-owned Instagram and Facebook. CNN spoke with over a dozen artists on how they are navigating the current AI landscape. AI-generated art profiles “monetize Facebook,” Burnham said. “They have hundreds of thousands of followers who believe these fake profiles are genuine artists and direct users to various websites with shops and ads.” The problem has pushed some independent artists to pull back from Instagram, Facebook and other Meta platforms, especially with the tech giant’s proposed updates to its terms of service. Some have considered leaving Meta-owned social media platforms entirely, pausing posting or turning to other online creator communities such as Patreon or Substack. Tim O’Brien, board member at the Society of Illustrators, said he believes artists deserve meaningful consent, fair compensation and accessible ways to challenge unauthorized exploitations of their work. “For many artists, this is not merely a legal dispute. It is a question of livelihood, creative ownership, consent and basic fairness,” O’Brien said. Meta’s updated terms would still allow automated software to scrape external websites and extract large amounts of data without permission from business account owners. This includes personal portfolios, online stores, and links to Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Threads business accounts. The terms were originally supposed to go into effect October 30, then got pushed back to November 20. The company announced on November 5 that the updates were delayed indefinitely. “We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect,” a Meta spokesperson said in a statement to CNN. Still, even with the latest delay, the proposed updates have already caused another wave of artists to leave Meta. Samantha Waldron, co-owner of Dutcher Photography in Madison, Wisconsin, told CNN that she deleted all business and personal Facebook pages earlier this month and has since transitioned her Instagram business accounts to personal accounts, deleted a vast majority of posts, and removed all external website links from Meta account bios. “It was the last straw that was a long time coming. I’m frankly relieved not to have to worry about keeping up on social media moving forward,” said Waldron. Under the updated terms, independent artists’ images, style, and property could be scraped without their knowledge to train generative AI models, creators told CNN. Those AI models could then replicate or replace human-made art — and potentially impact artists’ businesses on those sites. Megan Wimberley, founder of Cowgirl Artists of America in Tulsa, Oklahoma, is in the process of deleting all of her Meta accounts. She told CNN that she considers these new terms a major breach of trust. Wimberley believes everyone – not just artists – should be concerned about posting their personal images, video and audio due to potential AI scraping. “I actually view Meta as a company trying to lead the way in AI and that their social media platforms are no longer really about social media but more about free licensing to train their AI,” said Wimberley. “If you’re a mother and you’re posting your children, you’re potentially licensing Meta to use your children to train their AI.” Some even chose to “go dark” on Meta platforms from October 30 through November 6 when the updated Meta terms were initially planned to kick in, refraining from posting or sharing content in protest of the updated terms. Wimberley said she started the “Meta blackout” campaign on October 22, and it took off from there. Nicole McKay, artists relations director at The Guild of Artists and Artisans, told CNN in a statement that many artists in the United States have begun removing their accounts from Meta platforms in response to the upcoming policy change with AI model training. Many artists have posted “goodbye” messages on Instagram and Facebook, citing Meta’s politics. “For artists who rely on these platforms to showcase and sell their work, connect with customers, and build their businesses, leaving Meta presents a difficult choice between protecting their work and maintaining their livelihoods,” McKay said. Artists traverse ‘AI slop’ AI-generated artwork has serious repercussions on the creator economy, artists told CNN. Online imitators are forcing artists to change their strategy on how they reach an audience. Andrew Scott, a contemporary artist in Rochester, New York, said he directly messaged an AI art impersonator in September about copying his work. He said the person admitted to using Scott’s original work as a starting point to build her own AI-generated art videos. The person behind the impersonating profile then shared AI clips on Instagram, giving the impression she created the actual art. Scott noted one of her posts with AI artwork received 50 million views. Scott said he explained to the impersonator how the AI versions could potentially hurt his business. She has since unfollowed him on social media but continues to create the AI-prompted knockoffs, he said. Nancy Chen, a ceramic artist in Canada, posts videos on social media that show how she makes sale pieces. But she understands those clips could also be vulnerable to AI model training. Chen says she’s been wary lately of posting polished images of her work on Meta platforms but hasn’t decided to leave yet. “It makes me wonder how independent artists can present their work to the world when their transparency can be weaponized,” Chen told CNN. “AI can outpace any individual artist, so I definitely feel some pressure to compete in price, even though I feel my labor is already underpriced.” One of the main concerns for creators is the scale and speed that AI can push content, especially compared to human-made work that can be time-consuming. That concern is compounded by questions of how generative AI is trained on artwork, usually without artists’ say, and how copyright law applies to AI. Isaiah Steinfeld, an American Institute of Graphic Arts Board Member who builds with AI, said that protecting artists and embracing the technology don’t have to be opposing views. He noted that artists can still register work for copyright, pursue infringement claims and get unauthorized copies taken down. For instance, Meta said creators can report instances of AI impersonators and submit takedown requests via its Intellectual Property Reporting Center. “So, provenance has to cut both ways: protect creators from having their work appropriated and protect people using new (AI) tools from having their actual contributions erased,” Steinfeld said. Google released an online tool, SynthID Detector, this month to the public. The free site allows anyone to upload a file to check if that image, video or audio file was made by AI from Google and partners such as OpenAI, Nvidia and Kakao. In a press release, Google said the platform has watermarked over 180 million images and video and regularly sees over a million verification requests each day. But this is only the beginning, and independent artists agree these changes do not go far enough. Many still grapple with whether to share content on social platforms at all, but in their line of work, it’s about brand awareness. “Personally, I don’t trust that there will be enough done to protect artists,” Burnham said. “The UK government seems more concerned about not limiting profitable start-up tech companies than protecting artists. My hope is that the public continues to reject gen-AI in this current model.” When CNN reached out for comment, a spokesperson for the UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport said: “The government has engaged extensively with creatives, industry bodies and AI firms and we are taking time to ensure we find the right approach to this issue.” “We have been clear that we will not proceed with any course of action which does not work for our creative industries and our AI sector,” they added.

articles.title: US targeting India's manufacturing schemes while protecting its own industry through tariffs: GTRI
articles.summary: The United States is questioning India's manufacturing support initiatives, including the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme and Make in India, even
articles.body: The United States is questioning India's manufacturing support initiatives, including the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme and Make in India, even as it uses tariffs to protect its own manufacturing interests, Ajay Srivastava, founder of the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), has said.His remarks come after the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) proposed tariffs of up to 25% on Indian goods, citing structural excess manufacturing capacity. The proposed rate could be 17% if a trade deal is signed.Speaking to news agency ANI, Srivastava said Washington was criticising India's manufacturing policies because they could make domestic production more competitive and reduce demand for American goods."For India also, they listed all the schemes which India is using, and they are saying they are all hurting US manufacturers. So anything good you are doing in your country is hurting US manufacturing because, if you are making things in your country, US goods will sell less," he said.Srivastava argued that India was not the only country facing such scrutiny, with the US action covering 16 economies, including the European Union and China."They are targeting 16 economies. When I say economies, they target the European Union also, which has 27 countries. So almost all the big trading partners of the US have been targeted with high tariffs," he said.Referring to Cambodia, he said the USTR had also criticised its economic policies, labour laws and efforts to promote manufacturing.GTRI calls excess capacity claims a pretext for trade dealsSrivastava alleged that Washington was using concerns over excess manufacturing capacity to push countries towards trade agreements that favour the US."Excess capacities are just a pretence for an extractive one-sided trade deal," he said, arguing that the proposed tariffs were being used to pressure countries, including India, into signing trade agreements.He urged the Indian government to use the consultation period to present its case and explain why the country does not have structural excess capacity. According to Srivastava, the US has opened a window for consultations extending until January.He also asked India to highlight subsidies provided by the US to its agricultural sector while responding to the allegations."If you talk about agriculture, it is the US which subsidises its agriculture, so they have the most excess capacity. They have to look back into what they are doing also instead of accusing," he said.India says it has no structural excess capacityThe Union commerce and industry ministry has said India does not have structural excess capacity in any sector.The ministry said the USTR notice was under examination and that India had engaged constructively throughout the investigation."In response to the Notice of Initiation and in subsequent proceedings, the department of commerce stated that India does not have structural excess capacity in any sector," the ministry said.The proposed tariffs follow an eight-month investigation under Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974, which examined alleged unfair trade practices involving 16 trading partners.India has also maintained that trade-related concerns should be addressed through the ongoing negotiations for the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA)."India and the United States are engaged in negotiations for a Bilateral Trade Agreement. It has been India's position that any trade-related concerns should be addressed within the framework of these negotiations," the ministry said, reiterating the government's commitment to an early conclusion of the pact.Labour-intensive exports among those at riskSrivastava estimated that around 50-52% of India's exports to the US could be affected by the proposed tariffs. These include labour-intensive sectors such as textiles, leather, garments, handicrafts and some auto components.However, around 40% of India's exports, including diesel, petrol, generic medicines and iPhone-type products, would continue to enter the US at zero tariffs, he said.Steel, aluminium and copper, along with some auto components, would continue to face tariffs higher than 25%, currently at 50%. These products account for around 7-8% of India's exports to the US, according to Srivastava.The proposed tariffs cover economies including India, China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam, among others.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? Join the TOI Money Masterclass.

articles.title: Thanksgiving dinner costs rise, putting pressure on US households
articles.summary: Turkeys see a 26-percent price rise, forcing families to reconsider hosting and opt for potluck-style celebrations.
articles.body:
Across the United States, kitchens will fill with the smell of roasting turkey as Americans gather to celebrate the Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday.

Every family has its own traditions. Some swear by sweet potatoes topped with marshmallows. Others have carefully guarded family recipes for gravy, and there is always the perennial debate over pumpkin or pecan pie – and whether it should be served with a dollop of whipped cream or a scoop of ice cream.

But regardless of what makes it onto the Thanksgiving table this year, many Americans have something less appetising in common: a heftier grocery bill. The cost of a typical Thanksgiving meal is up 11 percent from last year, according to a new analysis by the think tank The Century Foundation.

The prices of many typical side dishes are up by double-digit percentages. Green beans are up 36.7 percent in price for a 1.5-pound bag, from $2.99 to $4.08 in a year’s time. Russet potatoes are up 6.8 percent for a five-pound bag, and Granny Smith apples, which are typically used in apple pie, are up 10.2 percent for a three-pound bag.

The centrepiece of the Thanksgiving table, the turkey, is also up by 26 percent compared with this time last year.

“Thanksgiving is supposed to be about gathering around the table, but this year many families are deciding how many people they can afford to feed,” Kyle Moore, chief economist at The Century Foundation, said in a statement.

Measuring just by the number of guests, the American Farm Bureau forecasts a rise of 6 percent for a 10-person meal, marking the first increase in price since 2022, when prices hit a record high, according to the report.

Some grocers are doing what they can to keep prices lower for consumers, including Baris Avci, who runs Green Valley, a small neighbourhood grocery store in the Bushwick neighbourhood of Brooklyn, New York.

“Some very important things like eggs, milk, sugar, we sell almost at cost. We don’t make much money, but we also have a certain percentage to [sustain] the business. Like how the people struggle, we struggle too,” Avci told Al Jazeera.

Higher prices mean that some shoppers are having to rethink their traditions. Sam Braverman, who was shopping at Green Valley, told Al Jazeera that in past years, his mother hosted Thanksgiving and took care of all the costs, but given price increases, his family is taking a different approach.

“Well, my ma is more open to kind of a potluck vibe this year, of people sort of bringing a few things,” Braverman told Al Jazeera.

“To make that same meal is going to be 130-150 percent of what it was last year, so you might as well accept some offerings.”

Heightened costs can stem from bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz because of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has led to a rise in the cost of both fuel and fertiliser needed in the food production supply chain.

During the spring planting season, prices for urea, which is used in fertilisers, jumped by as much as 50 percent when the war began, meaning that farmers needed to pay more for fertiliser. Those costs were ultimately passed down along the supply chain from farmers to warehouses and then onto supermarket shelves.

Tariff-driven pressures have also led to heightened costs. For example, tariffs on steel used in cans have caused prices to increase on canned goods for consumers. In September, Campbell’s Soup said it would raise prices by 4 to 5 percent on 60 percent of its products.

Some big-box retailers like Walmart, however, are using their economies of scale to cut prices for consumers. Every year, the Bentonville, Arkansas-based chain offers a holiday meal package that consumers can buy, which includes a complete holiday meal for 10 people. It will cost shoppers 12 percent less than the same deal last year.

For those bearing the brunt of the costs, that means more people are finding ways to borrow or at least scale back. A third of Americans who are planning on hosting this year say that doing so is putting them under financial strain, according to a report from LendingTree, an online loan marketplace.

As a result, nearly 62 percent of hosts say they’re going to borrow money to host this year – 18 percent of whom say they’re using what are called buy now, pay later (BNPL) loans, which are deferred payment plans for expenses.

Usage has jumped significantly in recent years, with 16 percent of Americans using BNPL loans, which are offered by fintech companies like Affirm and Klarna, marking a six-percentage-point jump since 2021, according to an August report from the US Federal Reserve.

It found that those with lower credit scores and lower incomes, as well as younger people and both Black and Hispanic adults, are more likely to use these services than the general population.

There are slightly fewer people travelling for Thanksgiving this year, too. The American Automobile Association (AAA) forecasts that more than 81.6 million Americans will travel, marking a slight decline of 121,000 travellers, including those travelling by plane, car, bus and train. The decline marks a reversal of the trend, as the number of travellers climbed over the last three years.

“After three years of record highs, the number of travelers is slightly lower, partly because of higher travel costs this year,” Stacey Barber, vice president of AAA Travel, said in a news release announcing the data.

Seven in 10 Americans are planning not to travel this holiday season at all, according to a report from the financial services company BNO, marking a 10-percent drop from this time last year.

While the average price for a gallon of petrol (3.78 litres) is down from last month – $3.61 on Tuesday versus $4.29 a month ago for regular fuel – it is still higher than this time last year, when it was $3.06, according to AAA’s daily fuel price tracker.

For those hitting the skies, domestic airfares rose 31 percent for Thanksgiving travel, averaging $402, according to a report released in September by the travel website Hopper, which tracks holiday travel trends, marking this Thanksgiving as the most expensive holiday travel season in a decade.

articles.title: At the gym with the CEO who made us wait 13 years for GTA VI
articles.summary: Strauss Zelnick’s quest for perfection offers a window into Take-Two’s unusual strategy for Grand Theft Auto VI.
articles.body: Strauss Zelnick strides on to the gym floor at 6:30 a.m. for a strength-training workout with the Program, the exercise group in New York City he created. He inspects each station, making sure the weights, repetitions and timing match the circuit he designed the night before. The 69-year-old CEO of Take-Two Interactive — the parent company behind Grand Theft Auto — is not a natural athlete. He was skinny well into his 30s. But Zelnick became a fitness fanatic, transformed his body and created the Program more than a decade ago. He typically exercises twice a day, using workouts as business and mentoring meetings. I have seen Zelnick’s relentless personal discipline up close. I knew him when I was a kid 25 years ago, and I’ve started working out with him and the Program over the last couple of years. Zelnick’s quest for perfection offers a window into Take-Two’s unusual strategy for Grand Theft Auto VI. The last installment of the Grand Theft Auto series came out 13 years ago. Most entertainment companies might have forced out a sequel long before, bowing to market pressure. But Zelnick doesn’t believe in doing things halfway. He was willing to endure three public delays on Grand Theft Auto VI, investor and fan angst, and sky-high expectations in pursuit of delivering something “exceptional.” “Consumers are not okay with okay,” he said in an interview with gaming site IGN last year. “Good is the new bad.” The strategy worked. Grand Theft Auto VI is poised to become the highest-earning intellectual property in entertainment history, eclipsing recent cultural phenomena like Taylor Swift’s Eras tour and The Odyssey. Getting out of the way I reach out to Zelnick for advice on health, exercise and my career every couple months. He responds almost immediately — as he does for anyone who seeks him out — even if it’s the morning of the Grand Theft Auto VI launch to decline my interview request for this article. Zelnick does not make video games or play them. It’s hard to imagine him with a controller in his hands. Instead, he is considered a master of identifying and managing highly creative people, with all their promise, brilliance and frustrations. He does this by creating corporate stability and giving them freedom to build great art. And then staying out of their way. Zelnick is not Jeff Bezos getting “heavily involved” in casting decisions about James Bond. “He knows what he knows, and he’s respectful of what he doesn’t,” said Jennifer Kolbe, the head of publishing at Rockstar Games, which makes Grand Theft Auto. It’s a management style Zelnick learned as a Hollywood wunderkind, the description of him that appeared in early public profiles in the 1990s. Intensely ambitious, Zelnick earned dual law and business degrees at Harvard before leaving his 20s. He became the head of Twentieth Century Fox by 32 and CEO of music recording giant BMG’s North America division by 37. Zelnick took control of Take-Two in 2007, when the company was on the brink of bankruptcy, under criminal investigation, and trading around $11 a share. (It’s at roughly $220 now.) “A lot of us at Rockstar worked within that mess at Take-Two,” said Kolbe, who has been at the company since 1996. “We stick by the premise that if (he) is going provide that stability, we’re going to provide hits.” Rockstar’s turnover is low, and roughly one in five employees has stayed with the company for more than a decade. (Rockstar has also been accused of firing dozens of employees to prevent them from unionizing. The company has said the firings were for misconduct.) Take-Two focused early under Zelnick on building out a handful of blockbuster franchises, including Red Dead Redemption, rather than churning out a constant stream of new games. “I’ve always believed the right strategy for an entertainment company is a limited number of very high-quality titles,” Zelnick told the website GamesBeat in 2008. Thousands of developers, artists, designers and other staff worked on Grand Theft Auto VI. Analysts estimated it will cost more than $1 billion — the most expensive video game ever — though Take-Two has not disclosed the figure. The mega-project stands out in an entertainment industry that has lost its appetite for expensive, time-consuming ventures. Most companies cut costs, shorten production cycles and try to pump out more with fewer resources to meet the pressures of Wall Street. Cautious corporate executives manage based on quarterly earnings targets or their own ideas about a movie script. “GTA VI is what happens when you provide the necessary financial resources to allow talented individuals to do their best work,” said Joost van Dreun, a professor at NYU Stern who studies gaming and tech. “There are few publishers that can stomach either the time horizon or the budget.” The Program Zelnick brings his obsession with structure to the gym. The Program trains in several high-end gyms around New York City a few times a week, everything paid for by Zelnick. Attending a workout requires only an invitation from one of the group’s roughly 300 members, a broad range from college students to executives in their 70s. His Program crew shows up year after year. People come to get in an hour-long workout and for the camaraderie. But they also go to develop a relationship with Zelnick, who has said he spends a quarter of his time mentoring and coaching. Zelnick is loyal, like when he recommended his shoulder surgeon to me nine minutes after I emailed him last November — “I’ve done endless research. No one else” — and reached out after the operation and during rehab. His quiet intensity can be intimidating, but I’ve found him surprisingly warm and self-deprecating. Zelnick’s motivation behind the Program is to build community, said Dan Harris, the host of the 10% Happier podcast and Zelnick’s close friend. His mother died when he was 10, his father abandoned the family and he was raised by his aunt and uncle. “What I see him doing with the Program is re-creating family,” Harris said. “The high standards and systems he puts in place are structures to create connection.” Zelnick designs most of the circuits, even when he’s on the road. After going over each station in person, he calls the group together. Everyone introduces themselves by name. Then Zelnick announces the exercises, time per station and number of reps. “Let’s go, team.” The workout begins promptly at 6:45 a.m. Like a trainer, he cheers you on and lets you know if you’re doing the wrong exercise or your form has slipped. But in a group Zelnick created and oversees, he delegates. One person leads the equipment setup. Another emails the weekly schedule out on Fridays. Someone else designs every workout playlist, with a heavy dose of Billy Joel’s “We Didn’t Start the Fire.” Zelnick seems almost incapable of small talk during the sessions, unless it’s to ask how you like the workout. He is locked in, constantly moving to achieve the next level.

articles.title: US authorizes SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites for AI data centers in space
articles.summary: The technology is central to SpaceX’s growth ambitions, though the company warned earlier this year that it relied on “unproven” technologies.
articles.body: The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk’s SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites in space for the creation of data centers critical to powering artificial intelligence. The decision comes as the US races to lead the world in AI, a technology that promises to turbocharge innovation and economic growth. Harnessing AI is also central to SpaceX’s growth ambitions, though the company cautioned in a regulatory filing ahead of its June initial public offering that launching data centers in space relied on “unproven” technologies and “may not achieve commercial viability.” Deploying SpaceX’s “Starmind” constellation – comprised of 1 million orbital compute modules – will help meet “rapidly growing demand” for AI computing power, the FCC said in a statement Wednesday. The deployed satellites will “process massive amounts of data to be used back here on Earth,” the agency added. “This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth,” said FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. AI data centers require enormous amounts of energy and Musk has endorsed orbital data centers that can harness the power of the sun. “By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost ​and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centers,” SpaceX ​told the FCC when it applied for permission to launch the satellites earlier this year. Musk welcomed the decision, saying on X, his social media platform, that “this will be a great asset to America and the world.” The initiative has drawn criticism from the scientific community, however, who have argued that the technology could disrupt views of the night sky and increase pollution. In a statement Wednesday, the American Astronomical Society said it was “dismayed” by the FCC’s decision, which it had opposed in earlier filings to the agency. The “proposed constellation would significantly undermine (i) decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and (ii) the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky,” the organization said. It noted that the satellites would be visible as “extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky” and would generate “radio emissions” and “waste heat” that would “threaten… sensitive instruments used in regular astronomy research.” It also warned of “atmospheric pollution” from the launches and reentries so many satellites. Under the license, SpaceX must deploy at least one authorized space station by November 2033, deploy 10% of the total – or 100,000 – by November 2035 and deploy 50% by November 2038. There are currently around 16,700 operational satellites in space, according to Orbital Radar, a platform providing real-time tracking of objects in orbit. The European Space Agency puts the number of functioning satellites slightly lower, at 15,800. Earlier this month, in a historic test flight, SpaceX’s Starship spacecraft deployed Starlink internet satellites before returning to earth and pulling of an unprecedented landing.

articles.title: Is UBI the solution to mass unemployment in an AI economy?
articles.summary: AI’s rapid advance has led to calls for universal payments to prevent poverty and wealth inequality.
articles.body:
As rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) raise fears of mass job losses, calls for the rollout of universal basic income (UBI) are gaining traction.

UBI is a regular cash payment made to every citizen regardless of employment status, income or wealth.

Proponents of UBI in the United States argue that governments should look to UBI to offset AI’s expected impact on the labour market and prevent extreme poverty and wealth inequality.

The idea of universal payments is not new.

In 1797, Thomas Paine, one of the key thinkers of the American Revolution, proposed an early version of UBI in a pamphlet titled Agrarian Justice. He argued that land was originally common property, shared by all of humanity. Those with no land, he said, were owed compensation as a basic human right.

Under Paine’s proposal, each person would have received a lump sum of 15 pounds when they turned 21, followed by an annual payment of 10 pounds from age 50, paid for by a tax on inherited property.

The idea resurfaced in the 1960s from opposing ends of the ideological spectrum.

US economist Milton Friedman proposed a “negative income tax”, under which the government would top up the earnings of anyone falling below a set threshold. Friedman, a champion of free-market policies, argued that his proposal would be cheaper than existing welfare programmes.

US civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr, in his 1967 book Where Do We Go from Here, called for a guaranteed income as a way to end poverty.

King Jr’s vision came close to being enshrined in law in 1969, when President Richard Nixon proposed the Family Assistance Plan, a minimum income for families with children. Nixon’s proposal passed the House of Representatives but stalled in the Senate, and the plan was eventually abandoned.

After falling out of fashion in subsequent decades, proposals for universal payments have re-entered the mainstream in recent years amid the rise of automation and AI.

Some of the loudest proponents of UBI are the people developing AI.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has been pushing the idea for years.

In a 2024 interview with the All-In Podcast, Altman proposed a twist on UBI that would give everyone a stake in the productive gains of AI.

“I wonder if the future looks something like more like universal basic compute than universal basic income and everybody gets like a slice of GPT 7’s compute and they can use it, they can resell it, they can donate it to somebody to use for cancer research,” Altman said, suggesting that citizens could “own part of the productivity” generated by AI instead of receiving cash.

In April, SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk said in an X post that a government-distributed “Universal High Income” would be the best way to deal with large-scale unemployment caused by AI.

Musk said AI and robotics would produce an abundance of goods and services far in excess of the increase in the money supply in future, so there would not be inflation.

Some observers have questioned the motivations of such proposals from billionaire tech executives.

Jonathan Portes, a professor of economics and public policy at King’s College, London, said tech leaders promoting UBI are acting out of “perceived self-interest”. In his view, a basic income could make job losses easier to accept as people are more likely to tolerate AI replacing their work if they are being paid.

“Partly it’s just another cool sounding idea,” Portes told Al Jazeera. “We should not take these people seriously on public policy issues at all.”

Most UBI proposals envision a system paid for by taxes, much in the same way as existing welfare programmes, though some pilot schemes have been funded by private donations.

Unlike traditional social welfare, which typically requires applicants to demonstrate financial hardship, UBI is paid to every member of a population without conditions.

Portes said UBI high enough to support acceptable living standards is not likely to be economically or politically viable in the near future.

While “a realistic UBI could help provide a better level of protection, increase individual autonomy and increase labour market flexibility, getting there would be complex”, he added.

“Many of the claims for it and fears are grossly exaggerated,” Portes said.

While everyone would get some financial benefit, some economists and technologists argue that the biggest beneficiary could be the economy.

In a scenario where AI leads to mass layoffs, people will have less money to spend. From this perspective, UBI would function less as a form of charity than as a way to keep consumer spending going.

That is the case made by Martin Ford, a futurist and the author of Rise of the Robots.

Ford argues that jobs are how purchasing power reaches common consumers, viewing UBI as a way to repair the link between production and spending rather than redistributing wealth for its own sake.

“Jobs are that mechanism that gets purchasing power to consumers so they can then drive the economy,” Ford said in a 2017 TED Talk.

“If, in fact, that mechanism begins to erode in the future, then we’re going to need to replace it with something else, or we’re going to face the risk that our whole system simply may not be sustainable.”

The most common objection is that unconditional cash discourages work. The evidence suggests the effect is real but modest.

In the biggest US trial of its kind, about 1,000 low-income participants were given $1,000 a month for three years.

OpenResearch’s Unconditional Cash Study, backed by OpenAI’s Altman, found that participants worked only 1.3-1.4 hours less each week compared with the control group.

More than half of recipients’ increased spending went on basic necessities such as food, housing and transport.

The study found no significant effect on physical health, and gains in wellbeing faded after the first year.

In the US, paying each family of four a universal payment of $30,000 – slightly below the official poverty line – would cost approximately $8.5 trillion each year, according to the Tax Project Institute.

That would dwarf current levels of spending on welfare.

The US government spent $1.7 trillion on some 90 welfare programmes in 2025, according to the conservative Heritage Foundation.
